section_summary: This section documents U.S. official and public concern over exports of strategic materials to Japan, including petroleum, copper, cobalt, zinc, scrap iron and steel, mercury, fluorspar, fusel oil, storage tanks, and industrial equipment. State Department memoranda assess Japanese stockpiling, possible re-export to Germany, weaknesses in existing export controls, and shipments from Latin America and the Philippines, while replies to citizens and legislators explain or defend current licensing policy. The section also contains advocacy correspondence supporting stronger economic pressure on Japan and aid to China, together with reports from Tokyo, London, Madrid, Mexico, Chile, and Peru.

subfiles.title: Continuation of memorandum on Japanese copper orders
subfiles.about: Compares copper quantities for 1938–1940 and warns that Japanese orders after the July embargoes indicate stockpiling.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page lists copper totals for 1938, 1939, and the first nine months of 1940. It emphasizes that roughly 150 million pounds were ordered after July 1940 and concludes that continued purchasing at that rate would be excessive.

subfiles.title: Cobalt Shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a large Belgian Congo cobalt cargo consigned to Mitsui and Mitsubishi and considers embargoing it.
subfiles.summary: The Barber Line vessel Westhumaw was expected to bring 426 metric tons of cobalt for Mitsui and 105 tons for Mitsubishi through Boston and New York. The amount equaled approximately a year's Japanese supply, raising suspicion that it might ultimately be intended for Germany. The memorandum also warns that Britain might otherwise seek to halt Belgian Congo cobalt trade with the United States.

subfiles.title: Record of Mr. Stannard's call concerning Japanese copper buying in Chile
subfiles.about: Records a copper-company representative's warning that Japanese trading houses might request introductions for copper negotiations in Chile.
subfiles.summary: Mr. Stannard reported that representatives of large Japanese houses such as Mitsui had invited him to lunch. He expected requests for letters of introduction to company officials in Chile and anticipated that the Japanese would approach Chilean authorities about their copper-buying program.

subfiles.title: Canadian reports on scrap iron and zinc procurement in Colombia
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Forwards Canadian Legation memoranda concerning Japanese efforts to obtain scrap iron and zinc through Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Green encloses memoranda relating to correspondence involving Canadian Metals Controller G. C. Bateman and F. H. Brownell. The enclosures also concern Stuart Hosie's approach to Fujiye Trading Company about scrap iron and I. Okura's report to Mitsui on Colombian zinc production.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department referral of Mata B. Roudin letter
subfiles.from: James W. Young, Director, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Refers Mata B. Roudin's letter about gasoline exports to the State Department for attention.
subfiles.summary: The Commerce Department transmits an attached letter to Joseph C. Green's office. It states that the writer has been advised of the referral.

subfiles.title: Routing sheets for Mata B. Roudin correspondence
subfiles.about: Summarizes and routes Roudin's inquiry about large gasoline shipments to Japan under government permits.
subfiles.summary: The two substantially duplicate sheets identify a December 8 letter from Mata B. Roudin of New York City. They request a direct reply regarding reports that large quantities of gasoline were being shipped to Japan under special permits.

subfiles.title: Letter questioning gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions continued gasoline shipments to Japan despite the government's export policy.
subfiles.summary: The letter is severely degraded in the OCR, but its routing description identifies the subject as large gasoline shipments to Japan under special government permits. Roudin asks the Secretary of Commerce for an explanation.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mata B. Roudin on gasoline regulations
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains that the July 1940 regulations prohibited only gasoline meeting the defined aviation-grade threshold.
subfiles.summary: Price states that only aviation gasoline was prohibited under regulations issued pursuant to the President's July 26 proclamation. He defines the threshold as an ASTM Knock Test octane rating of 87 or more, including gasoline capable of reaching that rating with limited tetraethyl lead. Shipments made since the prohibition were said not to meet those specifications.

subfiles.title: Exports of crude oil and gasoline to Japan through December 1940
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports a December surge in gasoline exports to Japan and supplies monthly petroleum export figures.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes that gasoline exports rose sharply in December while crude-oil exports declined. Much of the gasoline was medium-grade aviation fuel that could be converted easily into higher-quality fuel. A table compares the first eight months of 1940 with September through December and also gives annual totals for 1939.

subfiles.title: Petroleum exports, outstanding licenses, and related equipment
subfiles.about: Reviews Japanese petroleum imports, outstanding export licenses, and possible controls on drums, tanks, and oil-field equipment.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that nearly 3.5 million barrels of gasoline went to Japan in 1940, with most shipped in the final four months, while approximately four million barrels remained authorized under valid licenses. Much of the fuel was usable in Japanese military aircraft or could be upgraded easily, and some license applications expressly named the Imperial Japanese Navy or Army. Yost discusses lowering the permitted octane threshold, restricting exports to prewar levels, and extending licensing to metal drums, storage tanks, and drilling equipment reportedly reaching Germany through Japan.

subfiles.title: War Department transmittal of Dr. King's letter
subfiles.to: Cecil W. Gray, Department of State
subfiles.about: Forwards George S. King's inquiry about exports to Japan for State Department action.
subfiles.summary: Martyn states that Secretary Stimson received a letter from Dr. George S. King of Bay Shore. King was advised that the issue belonged with the State Department and asked that the letter be forwarded.

subfiles.title: Dr. King's protest against gasoline and armor-plate exports
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Protests alleged exports of gasoline and armor plate to Japan and suspected transshipment through Mexico.
subfiles.summary: King argues that commercial gasoline could be converted into aviation fuel and later used against the United States. He also questions reports that Japan could purchase armor plate and that scrap iron and oil were being sent through Mexico for transshipment. He asks Stimson to explain what he regards as an irrational and dangerous policy.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to George S. King
subfiles.from: Leonard H. Price, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Assures King that export licenses are reviewed for national-defense concerns and denies the reported armor-plate and Mexican transshipment claims.
subfiles.summary: Price says the relevant agencies continuously study exports governed by the Export Control Act. He reports that no license had been issued during the year for armor plate to Japan. The Department also had no reason to believe that scrap iron and oil exported to Mexico had been unlawfully transshipped to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum summarizing J. Leighton Stuart's circular
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Sumner Welles, and the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Summarizes Stuart's appeal for comprehensive economic pressure on Japan and his assessment of possible Japanese responses.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports that Americans in North China strongly approved restrictions on scrap exports and hoped for wider economic measures compelling Japan to withdraw from China and abandon southward expansion. Stuart foresaw continued aggression, genuine retrenchment, or tactical concessions intended to weaken American resolve. He urged the United States to maintain its stand despite the risk of conflict.

subfiles.title: Roger S. Greene's forwarding letter for Stuart circular
subfiles.about: Forwards Leighton Stuart's October 19 circular and recommends that it be shown to Secretary Hull.
subfiles.summary: Greene describes Stuart's circular as worthy of special consideration and asks Hornbeck to present it to Secretary Hull. He praises Stuart's far-sighted attitude toward the difficult circumstances confronting Yenching University's community in North China.

subfiles.title: Confidential circular to the Board of Trustees of Yenching University
subfiles.to: Board of Trustees of Yenching University
subfiles.about: Advocates sustained American economic pressure on Japan and describes the dangers facing Yenching University.
subfiles.summary: Stuart endorses the prohibition of steel and scrap-iron sales and urges broader restrictions until Japan withdraws from China and abandons further expansion. He analyzes three possible Japanese responses and warns particularly against superficial concessions designed to weaken American resolve. He also describes evacuation planning, concern over university property, possible Japanese seizure or looting, and the determination of American staff to remain as long as possible.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene's letter and states that Stuart's circular is being circulated within the Department.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Greene for sending the confidential October 19 letter from Leighton Stuart. He says he has noted Stuart's views with interest and is passing the letter to other Department officers.

subfiles.title: Illegible separator page
subfiles.about: Contains no recoverable substantive document text.
subfiles.summary: Only a short stray OCR fragment is visible on this page. No subject, author, recipient, or date can be identified.

subfiles.title: Orrin G. Judd letter on exports to Japan and Brooklyn meeting
subfiles.about: Urges expansion of the embargo and requests a State Department speaker for a Brooklyn meeting on China.
subfiles.summary: Judd says Brooklyn residents cannot understand continued exports of copper, oil, oil products, and machinery used in Japan's war against China. He asks Hull to press the President for wider restrictions. He also invites the Department to send a representative to a December 14 meeting at the Central YMCA in Brooklyn.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Orrin G. Judd
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains current export controls and declines to send an officer to Judd's Brooklyn meeting.
subfiles.summary: Allen encloses the Export Control Act and related proclamations and regulations, noting that scrap iron and steel, aviation gasoline, and lubricating oil were restricted to the Western Hemisphere and Great Britain. He says further restrictions remained under continuing consideration. Because of the Department's workload, no officer could attend the December 14 luncheon.

subfiles.title: Brooklyn Committee letter demanding an explanation of Japan trade policy
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States continues supplying Japan and requests a speaker or policy statement for a Brooklyn conference.
subfiles.summary: Boulton welcomes the loan to China and limited refusals of export licenses but asserts that the United States still supplied most materials Japan needed for war. She cites public opposition and reports that armor-plate producers wanted the government to relieve them of Japanese contracts. She requests either a speaker or a written policy statement for a December 14 meeting featuring Ben Cowles.

subfiles.title: Says Japan Gets Zinc Needed Here
subfiles.from: Associated Press report quoting C. Donald Dallas
subfiles.about: Reports that zinc exports to Japan were causing shortages for American and British brass production.
subfiles.summary: Dallas states that 3,775 tons of zinc went to Japan in October and 12,042 tons during the first ten months of 1940. He argues that domestic brass plants were curtailing defense production because zinc needed for cartridge cases, detonator caps, fuses, and other armament components had been exported. He recommends finding new supplies or diverting zinc from decorative consumer uses.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Frances S. Boulton
subfiles.from: Edgar P. Allen, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the export-control framework and declines to provide a Department speaker for the December 14 luncheon.
subfiles.summary: The damaged first page nevertheless parallels the Department's reply to Judd and encloses the Export Control Act and implementing measures. Allen says restrictions vary according to American defense needs and remain under continuing study. He declines the luncheon invitation because of the Department's heavy workload.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price cover letter to Maxwell Hamilton
subfiles.about: Forwards a copy of Price's letter to Export Control Administrator Russell L. Maxwell.
subfiles.summary: Price sends Hamilton a copy of his recent letter to Colonel Russell L. Maxwell. The enclosure concerns the adequacy and administration of export controls on materials going to Japan.

subfiles.title: Price letter criticizing limited export controls
subfiles.about: Urges wider licensing of war materials and questions Maxwell's apparent effort to minimize existing restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Price argues that the Export Control Act permits withholding strategic materials from potential enemies and that public opinion strongly favors broader restrictions on Japan. He stresses the contradiction between aiding Chinese resistance and permitting Japan to purchase materials for military expansion. Citing zinc shortages and newspaper reports, he asks whether Maxwell's statements accurately reflect an intention to limit the effect of export controls.

subfiles.title: Oil Export Control May Bar Only Plane Fuel
subfiles.from: New York Herald Tribune / Associated Press
subfiles.about: Reports Maxwell's effort to confine petroleum controls to aviation fuel and discusses possible licensing of zinc.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says Maxwell sought to minimize disruption to petroleum exports by restricting controls to fuel and oil used exclusively in aircraft. It also reports official study of zinc controls following C. Donald Dallas's warning that shipments to Japan were delaying domestic brass production. An informed source suggested zinc might soon be made subject to export licensing.

subfiles.title: Charge slip for file 894.24/1205
subfiles.about: Records the temporary charging-out of document 894.24/1205.
subfiles.summary: The standardized State Department form identifies file number 894.24/1205. It contains a charge date and clerk notation but no substantive discussion of export policy.

subfiles.title: Internal routing instructions concerning the Lazaron correspondence
subfiles.from: Office of the Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Directs preparation and routing of a reply concerning the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel.
subfiles.summary: The fragmentary typed and handwritten notes ask the Division of Controls to draft a response. The proposed routing appears to call for the draft to pass through Far Eastern Affairs before returning to the senior official.

subfiles.title: Welles note requesting Hornbeck's advice
subfiles.about: Asks what reply should be made to Morris S. Lazaron.
subfiles.summary: Welles forwards or references Lazaron's inquiry and asks Hornbeck for advice on the response. The note forms part of the internal handling of Lazaron's invitation from the scrap-iron trade organization.

subfiles.title: Lazaron request for advice about scrap-industry banquet
subfiles.about: Requests counsel on whether to deliver the invocation at the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel banquet.
subfiles.summary: Lazaron says he has been invited to give the invocation at the institute's January convention in Baltimore. He is hesitant because he does not know whether the industry is cooperating with the Administration and because he dislikes the nature of the trade. Although inclined to refuse, he asks Welles for advice before deciding.

subfiles.title: Welles reply regarding the Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel
subfiles.about: Advises Lazaron that the scrap-industry institute cooperated with the government and that he need not decline its invitation.
subfiles.summary: Welles says press portrayals of the scrap-iron industry as uniquely obstinate were unfair because most industries continued Far Eastern exports until prohibited. He reports that the institute offered admirable assistance during consultations preceding the scrap-export ban. He therefore sees no reason for Lazaron to refuse the invocation invitation.
keywords: Institute of Scrap Iron and Steel

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Mr. Buffum on aviation gasoline policy
subfiles.about: Records Buffum's criticism of policy toward Japanese refinery plants and aviation-gasoline exports.
subfiles.summary: Buffum argued that permitting Japan to buy refinery plants could have depleted its foreign exchange while the United States later withheld essential catalysts, leaving the plants useless. Instead, Japan had spent its money stockpiling gasoline capable of producing fuel rated at 90 octane or higher. He suggested quietly changing testing specifications to reduce the quality exportable under existing licenses.

subfiles.title: Senator Johnson's transmittal of Colorado organizations' telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards a protest concerning an alleged shipment of scrap-iron billets to Japan and requests a prompt report.
subfiles.summary: Johnson transmits a message from the Colorado Friends of the Chinese People and the Denver Chapter of the American Bureau for Medical Aid to China. He asks the Secretary of State for prompt advice so that he can report back to the organizations.

subfiles.title: Telegram alleging shipment of scrap billets to Japan
subfiles.from: Colorado Friends of the Chinese People and Denver Chapter, American Bureau for Medical Aid to China
subfiles.about: Alleges that 86 carloads of scrap iron were melted into billets to evade the export ban and loaded for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The organizations ask Johnson to stop a shipment allegedly prepared by the Minnequa Plant of the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. They claim scrap iron was converted into billets to evade the ban and loaded on December 20 aboard the Tosei Maru for Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Senator Johnson on alleged billet shipment
subfiles.about: Reports that the alleged export-license application could not be identified and encloses the December 10 iron-and-steel regulations.
subfiles.summary: Hull says officials searched the large body of export-license applications but could not identify the shipment from the limited details supplied. He encloses the President's December 10 proclamation and regulations governing iron and steel products. The reply explains that licenses remained available for the Western Hemisphere and, where national-defense interests permitted, other destinations.

subfiles.title: Fusel oil uses and possible Japanese stockpiling
subfiles.from: Jones, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Explains fusel oil's industrial and military uses and recommends circulating the Tokyo report to relevant agencies.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies fusel oil chiefly with amyl alcohol and describes its use in paints, lacquers, airplane dope, and potentially smokeless powder. It interprets rising Japanese purchases as possible stockpiling or procurement for Germany, with the latter considered more likely. Copies of the attached telegram are recommended for naval, military, export-control, and Commerce officials.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on increased fusel-oil shipments
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports unusually large American fusel-oil shipments to Japan and continued Mitsui purchasing above market prices.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy reports that shipments categorized as other alcohols including fusel oil reached 1,878,200 pounds in the first eleven months of 1940. This compared with 928,700 pounds in the corresponding 1939 period and 453,700 pounds in 1938. Mitsui was reportedly continuing to buy large quantities at twenty percent above current market prices.

subfiles.title: Paraphrases of Tokyo fusel-oil telegram
subfiles.about: Provides two paraphrased copies of the Embassy's report on Japanese fusel-oil purchases.
subfiles.summary: The copies restate the Tokyo Embassy's warning that shipments of fusel oil from the United States to Japan had increased sharply. They reproduce the comparative figures for 1938–1940 and report that Mitsui continued purchasing at twenty percent above the prevailing market price.

subfiles.title: British Embassy report on oil-storage tanks exported to Japan
subfiles.about: Records a British Embassy statement about a large December shipment of petroleum-storage tanks to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes that Mr. Butler, Mr. Hill, and he discussed the issue on January 6. Hill stated that tanks or tank materials exported on December 21, mostly for 9,000-barrel units, could store approximately 1.1 million barrels of petroleum products.

subfiles.title: London telegram on British refusal of Japanese tank gear-box exports
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, American Embassy London
subfiles.about: Reports British controversy over and final refusal of an export license for gear-box parts intended for Japan.
subfiles.summary: British newspapers reported worker protests after evidence emerged that factory products were destined for Japanese military use. Investigation found that a prewar contract covered gear boxes of a type used in Japanese tanks, with many larger parts already shipped and paid for. The Export Licence Department refused permission for the remaining parts, leaving goods valued at about £17,500 useless despite expected Japanese protests.

subfiles.title: Antofagasta despatch on copper shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: George H. Adams, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: Reports large January–February copper shipments from Antofagasta to Japan and encloses a detailed sailing schedule.
subfiles.summary: Adams reports that the Chile Exploration Company planned to ship 12,720 long tons of copper to Japan and 11,350 tons to the United States. The sudden Japanese demand for semi-refined copper aroused local suspicion because earlier purchases had been limited to low-grade ore. The confidential enclosure lists vessels, dates, destinations, tonnage, and forms of copper bound for New York, Yokohama, Osaka, and Japan generally.

subfiles.title: Voorhis inquiry about crude oil mixed with Ethyl
subfiles.about: Relays an allegation that Standard Oil in California was mixing crude oil with Ethyl and selling it to Japan as crude.
subfiles.summary: Voorhis says he has no proof of the report but believes it important enough for investigation. The allegation concerns equal parts crude oil and “Ethyl,” with the mixture allegedly classified and sold as crude oil to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Voorhis on crude-oil mixtures
subfiles.about: Explains licensing rules for crude oil mixed with tetraethyl lead, aviation lubricant, or Ethyl gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Hull says Voorhis's letter does not clarify whether “Ethyl” means Ethyl gasoline or tetraethyl lead. No licenses had authorized tetraethyl lead, aviation lubricating oil, or aviation gasoline exports to Japan, and customs officials would not release crude mixed with those controlled products without licenses. Crude mixed with Ethyl gasoline could be exported only if the gasoline remained below the specified aviation-fuel octane threshold.

subfiles.title: Madrid telegram on Japanese purchase of Spanish mercury
subfiles.from: Alexander W. Weddell, American Embassy Madrid
subfiles.about: Reports Mitsubishi's purchase of 253 flasks of mercury from the Spanish Almadén mines.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source reported that the Almadén mines had sold Mitsubishi 253 additional flasks of mercury valued at 63,250. The lot was expected to travel from Vigo to Yokohama via New York aboard the Artigas.

subfiles.title: Exportation of Fluorspar Ore From Mexico
subfiles.from: Pierre de L. Boal, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports a proposed Japanese contract for monthly shipments of Mexican fluorspar through Acapulco.
subfiles.summary: A Mexico City customs-brokerage firm reportedly contracted to deliver 5,000 tons of fluorspar ore monthly to a Japanese purchaser at Acapulco. William R. Hamer confirmed seeing the contract and said General Motors' New York office refused to sell the thirty trucks sought for moving the ore. The report describes rich mines near Taxco and Zacualpan and the possible road route to Acapulco, with NYK reportedly financing the ore purchases.

subfiles.title: Clinton letter on Philippine ore exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls attention to Philippine exports of iron, copper, manganese, and chrome ore to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Clinton cites a Manila Bulletin report that Philippine Iron Mines shipped 29,383 tons of high-grade iron ore to Japan in December. He also names reported shipments of chrome and copper by other Philippine companies. Warning that the ores might return as Japanese munitions, he urges measures to stop or curtail the trade.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Delmar S. Clinton
subfiles.from: John C. Davis, Office of Philippine Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks Clinton for reporting Philippine mineral exports and notes that the Department monitors Philippine export figures.
subfiles.summary: Davis acknowledges Clinton's January 23 letter to the Secretary of State. He says the Department is following Philippine export statistics but welcomes information of the kind Clinton supplied.

subfiles.title: Senator Bone's transmittal of McRae letter
subfiles.about: Forwards McRae's complaint about copper trolley wire allegedly destined for Japan and requests return of the enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Bone sends Hull a letter from W. E. McRae of Seattle for consideration. He asks that the original be returned after the Department has noted its contents.

subfiles.title: McRae letter on Seattle trolley wire exports
subfiles.about: Alleges that old Seattle trolley wire could evade the scrap ban by being smelted into ingots for Japan.
subfiles.summary: McRae reports being told that many tons of old copper trolley wire would be sent to the Tacoma smelter because it could not be exported as scrap. Once melted into ingots, it could allegedly be shipped to Japan. He argues that this practice conflicts with the President's call for the democracies to stand together.

subfiles.title: Negotiations of Japanese Interests to Purchase Petroleum in Peru
subfiles.from: J. F. McGurk, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.about: Reports inquiries into alleged Japanese negotiations for Peruvian petroleum and oil-field surveys.
subfiles.summary: The International Petroleum Company's Lima manager confirmed that his company had discussed the reported contract in New York but had heard nothing further after returning to Peru. He knew of no Sano Bussan representative arriving to survey Peruvian oil fields. Peru's Foreign Office and Ministry of Commerce and Industry likewise denied knowledge of such Japanese activity.

subfiles.title: Review of application to export 4.5 million gallons of gasoline to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Reviews a gasoline export application destined for Japanese naval refining and recommends no change in existing policy.
subfiles.summary: The application covered 4.5 million gallons whose specifications did not require refusal under current directives. The document nevertheless notes that the gasoline was intended for the Japanese Navy and could be refined to yield fuel above 87 octane. Far Eastern Affairs found no new regional circumstance justifying a policy change.

subfiles.title: Editorial survey on American Pacific policy
subfiles.about: Begins reporting a statistical analysis of 939 newspaper editorials on American policy in the Pacific.
subfiles.summary: Price says the committee reviewed editorials from 233 newspapers in 105 communities across 38 states during September 12–October 26, 1940. The surviving page begins a breakdown of attitudes toward aid to China, including general, financial, and munitions assistance. The letter continues beyond this section.
